biography.name: Colton Reed

background.family: Lives with his father and grandmother; his mother lives elsewhere and calls irregularly.
background.finances: Basic expenses are usually covered, but unexpected repairs consume savings. He has a small amount from weekend chores.
background.geography: Outside a small town near Childress in the Texas Panhandle.
background.cultureLanguages: English-speaking extended family with strong local ties and frequent teasing that he does not always enjoy.
background.school: Small public high school; several activities share one afternoon bus.
background.accessOpportunities: Neither parent attended college. His grandmother keeps school paperwork organized. Colton has ADHD and describes losing track of materials even for activities he wants to do.

timeline.story: Colton wanted to carry a flashlight during every evening walk with his grandmother, even before dark. He collected smooth stones and abandoned them in coat pockets. At home he enjoyed cooking scrambled eggs with help but refused to taste the tomatoes his father kept offering him.

He and a friend swapped trading cards at recess, arguing about bent corners and whether a shiny card was really rare. Colton sometimes accepted a trade too quickly and regretted it later. He also loved a classroom singing game despite insisting at home that singing was embarrassing.

His father brought home a box of secondhand sports equipment. Colton cleaned several items and compared them with pictures in store flyers. He was disappointed that a carefully scrubbed glove still smelled musty. He played baseball that spring, then became more interested in bicycling with two neighbors.

For a school project he compared the price and quantity of several packages of seeds. He liked noticing that the largest package was not always cheapest per packet. The presentation arrived a day late because he left it on the kitchen table, a problem his good calculations did not solve.

He tried selling a few cleaned secondhand game accessories to people his family knew. One item did not work consistently, and refunding the buyer used most of what he had earned. He disliked admitting the mistake and avoided another sale for months, while continuing to browse listings for fun.

Colton compared three offers for supplies used at a school booth, including delivery costs that a friend initially ignored. He also underestimated how many boxes they could carry. His ADHD was already known at school; a checklist helped with some handoffs, but he still forgot it when rushing.

He is experimenting with occasional resale of used board games, checking missing pieces at the kitchen table. He enjoys comparing what different sellers include and is less interested in photographing each box. A recent game has attracted no buyers. He alternates between lowering its price and deciding he might keep it.

enjoys: Comparing offers including hidden costs
Bicycling on familiar roads
Checking secondhand games for missing pieces
avoids: Admitting an item was a poor purchase
demonstratedSkills: Comparing quantities and total prices
Spotting differences in what sellers include
Testing used items before another person receives them
unfamiliarActivities: Keeping records for an entire year
Buying a large quantity of anything
Managing transactions with strangers at a distance
motivations: Having his own spending money
Finding something other people overlooked
Being trusted after a mistake
ambitions: Save for a dependable used vehicle
Try a larger town for a while
Have more control over his weekly schedule
struggles: Can conceal mistakes until asked directly
supports: A teacher who checks that he recorded instructions
practicalConstraints: Unfamiliarity with options after high school

biography.selfDescription: Comparing stuff is interesting. Posting it and waiting for answers is mostly annoying. People act like those are the same activity.
openQuestions: Will he keep wanting to do the less interesting parts?
How much financial uncertainty can he tolerate without withdrawing?

biography.name: Tessa McBride

background.family: Splits weekdays and weekends between divorced parents; has an older half brother she rarely sees.
background.finances: Both homes are comfortable, though parents disagree about which optional expenses they should share.
background.geography: Fort Worth, Texas, with two households on opposite sides of the city.
background.cultureLanguages: English-speaking; family gatherings mix differing political views and she dislikes being asked to take a side.
background.school: Public high school with many clubs and an active student council.
background.accessOpportunities: Has reliable internet and rides most weeks; a parent attended college and assumes she will attend too.

timeline.story: Tessa made her stuffed animals sit through announcements about the day's pretend picnic. She liked deciding what came first, while a neighbor preferred drawing invitations. Their games sometimes ended when Tessa insisted on changing the story after everyone had already chosen a role for themselves.

She enjoyed classroom show and tell, especially choosing the first sentence that would make people look up. She tried piano lessons because her brother played, but repeated practice frustrated her. A homemade birthday invitation interested her more for its wording than for the crooked letters and pictures.

When her parents separated, Tessa began keeping separate bags at both homes and frequently forgot something important anyway. She took comfort in planning elaborate weekend visits with a friend. She also started making short pet videos, although most stayed unfinished after she lost interest in editing.

Her class collected books, and Tessa noticed that asking for funny books brought different donations than asking for books generally. She liked trying both messages. She disliked arranging the display and convinced another child to do it, then felt annoyed when that child changed the title without consulting her.

She helped promote a school clothing exchange and wanted separate messages for students and parents. Some classmates thought she was making a simple task too complicated. Her first announcement sounded preachy when read aloud, so she rewrote it after a friend laughed at one sentence she had considered excellent.

Tessa joined a student election campaign because she liked deciding what the candidate should emphasize to different groups. She asked an artistic friend to handle the visuals and then kept requesting revisions too late. The candidate lost. Tessa enjoyed discussing which messages reached people more than discussing the final vote.

She is helping publicize a school event with a smaller team. She interviews classmates about why they might skip it and keeps suggesting changes to the invitation. She still delegates artwork. This time she agreed to an earlier deadline, but managing the two household calendars has already caused one missed meeting.

enjoys: Choosing a campaign's central message
Thinking about who will read an announcement
Trying different opening sentences
demonstratedSkills: Adapting wording for different audiences
Asking why people might decline an invitation
Spotting a confusing announcement
unfamiliarActivities: Tracking whether messages change behavior over time
motivations: Making people pay attention
Having her ideas used
Understanding why one approach works better
ambitions: Help make an event people actually attend
Spend a summer away from both households
Make something she finishes and can show friends
struggles: Two household schedules cause missed commitments
supports: An artistic friend who sets limits
A club sponsor who insists on deadlines
Both parents provide practical help when asked early

biography.selfDescription: I know when something sounds like an announcement nobody will read. I am less good at agreeing that it is finished.
openQuestions: How will she respond when a simple message succeeds without her preferred changes?
Can she give collaborators enough time and ownership?

biography.name: Gabriel Soto

background.family: Lives with his mother and aunt; an older cousin nearby is his usual sounding board.
background.finances: Modest but predictable household income; optional purchases and trips need advance saving.
background.geography: El Paso, Texas, in a neighborhood with several generations of extended family nearby.
background.cultureLanguages: Uses English and Spanish daily, reading more quickly in English; family members often disagree vigorously over dinner.
background.school: Public high school with a small discussion club and a library he uses during lunch.
background.accessOpportunities: Internet is reliable, but there is one shared laptop. His aunt attended college and can explain some procedures, although she is often unavailable during the week.

timeline.story: Gabriel asked adults why signs on the same street used different words for similar things. He liked being read stories with repeated phrases and corrected anyone who skipped one. He was also impatient with puzzles, sometimes pushing pieces together until his aunt persuaded him to look at their shapes.

He liked a classroom game where children decided whether a statement about an animal could be true. He would bring up exceptions long after everyone else moved on. During a school performance he forgot a short line and became determined to avoid the next performance, despite enjoying rehearsals with friends.

A disagreement about a game rule led him to read the entire instruction booklet and mark the relevant sentence. He won that argument but discovered his cousin no longer wanted to play. Around the same time he became enthusiastic about drawing maps, then stopped when he found shading them tedious.

Gabriel read two conflicting explanations of a local water restriction and asked his aunt which details each left out. She encouraged him but grew tired of discussing it every evening. He began writing paragraphs in a notebook, enjoying the chance to revise a sentence before anyone could respond.

In class he wrote a careful response to a disputed school rule and was upset when a teacher said his tone sounded contemptuous. He revised it reluctantly. He tried a speaking competition once, disliked waiting under the lights, and found that remembering his points did not prevent his voice from shaking.

He joined a discussion club that allowed written contributions. He compared competing claims about a community issue, separating the factual disagreements from different priorities. Friends appreciated his explanations but sometimes wanted him to stop correcting minor wording. He also took up casual jogging because it required little conversation or equipment.

Gabriel is writing a longer piece about a contested school policy, checking quotations against original documents when he can find them. He enjoys constructing a reasoned argument and dislikes imagining himself presenting it aloud. He has delayed sharing the draft because one missing fact bothers him, and he knows he may be using that gap as cover.

enjoys: Reading competing accounts
Building a written argument
Jogging familiar routes
Revising a paragraph until its meaning is precise
avoids: Being asked for an instant opinion
demonstratedSkills: Comparing conflicting claims
Checking quotations against a source
Distinguishing factual disagreement from differing priorities
unfamiliarActivities: Speaking to a large audience regularly
motivations: Understanding what can be supported
Being taken seriously
Avoiding an argument based on a careless claim
ambitions: Publish something classmates choose to read
Become less defensive about feedback
Visit a place he has only read about
struggles: Can sound dismissive when correcting details
Shaky public delivery makes him withdraw
supports: An aunt who discusses sources when free
A cousin who gives blunt feedback
A club sponsor accepting written participation

biography.selfDescription: A claim can sound obvious until you ask what would count as evidence against it. I also know saying that at dinner can be annoying.
openQuestions: Will he share work before every uncertainty is resolved?
How does he respond when a careful argument changes nobody's mind?

biography.name: Jules Carter

background.family: Lives with their father, grandmother, and younger cousin, who is staying with them for an uncertain length of time.
background.finances: Income is adequate in most months, with little room for replacing lost equipment or paying unexpected activity fees.
background.geography: Houston, Texas, in a neighborhood where weather and traffic can quickly disrupt plans.
background.cultureLanguages: English-speaking Black family with a wide network of relatives, church acquaintances, and longtime neighbors; Jules participates selectively.
background.school: Large public high school with many student groups and frequent timetable changes.
background.accessOpportunities: Can reach school activities by bus, but weekend travel depends on adults. Their grandmother provides steadiness while their father has an unpredictable schedule.

timeline.story: Jules gathered neighborhood children for sidewalk games and changed the rules whenever someone arrived late. They liked having everyone included but became bossy when other children wanted a different game. Indoors they enjoyed listening to their grandmother's stories and seldom finished the coloring pages she offered afterward.

On a rainy birthday afternoon Jules proposed moving the planned outdoor games into a hallway. They assigned jobs confidently and forgot that someone needed to move breakable objects first. An adult intervened. Jules remembered the successful new game much more clearly than the cleanup their cousins had to do.

They wanted to learn drumming and practiced on borrowed equipment for several months. Carrying it between homes became inconvenient, and the interest faded. At school they liked assigning parts for group stories, although their friends objected when Jules changed the ending without telling the person writing it down.

A cancelled bus disrupted a class outing, and Jules helped friends sort out who could wait and who needed an adult called. They liked finding an immediate workable plan. The following week they lost the permission slip for another activity and missed it, something they found unfair despite accepting responsibility later.

Jules began helping with neighborhood gatherings, usually volunteering when something changed at the last minute. They could quickly ask people to move tables or share materials. They disliked counting supplies afterward and left that task to an irritated cousin, who said being good in a scramble did not excuse disappearing during cleanup.

At a school event, a room change forced two groups into one smaller space. Jules got representatives together, proposed a shorter sequence, and delegated seating and signs. The event proceeded, but they had promised both groups the final time slot. Repairing that conflict took longer than the original emergency.

Jules is helping coordinate a student gathering while also agreeing to assist a family celebration on the same weekend. They enjoy making decisions when weather or attendance changes and delegate detailed lists. They have started writing commitments on their phone, though they sometimes accept a new request before checking what is already there.

enjoys: Finding a workable plan when circumstances change
Getting people to make a decision
Family storytelling
Busy gatherings with a concrete purpose
demonstratedSkills: Gathering decision makers quickly
Dividing urgent work among available people
Adjusting a sequence when space or attendance changes
unfamiliarActivities: Maintaining plans for a yearlong project
Managing a team without an immediate problem
motivations: Keeping people from feeling stranded
Being trusted when something goes wrong
Enjoying the energy of a shared task
ambitions: Complete an event without disappointing a second group
Have greater independence over transport
Keep enough unplanned time for friends
supports: A cousin willing to help when duties are explicit
A school advisor who makes them record agreements
practicalConstraints: Limited funds to replace missing materials

biography.selfDescription: If the plan falls apart, tell me what we still have. If you want me to remember the exact number of napkins next month, remind me twice.
openQuestions: Can they keep commitments manageable without losing the energy they enjoy?
Will collaborators accept their delegation when no emergency makes it feel necessary?

biography.name: Jordan Fuentes

background.family: Lives with their mother and mother’s partner; sees their father some weekends, with changing arrangements.
background.finances: Bills are usually covered, but replacing broken devices takes negotiation and saving.
background.geography: San Antonio apartment complex near a busy arterial road.
background.cultureLanguages: English and conversational Spanish; different relatives use different names and pronouns for them.
background.school: Large public school with an introductory computing class and a crowded device checkout program.
background.accessOpportunities: Uses a refurbished laptop; an older cousin shares explanations by voice message, but home support varies.

timeline.story: Jordan liked pressing the same button on a toy cash register until they understood which drawer movement followed it. They also made elaborate blanket forts with cousins. Their mother remembers constant questions; Jordan remembers mostly wanting adults to stop answering questions they had not asked.

They discovered that changing a saved game name did not change the name displayed everywhere. An uncle explained that separate places could store separate copies. Jordan forgot most of his explanation but remembered the annoyance, and began looking for other things that updated in one place but not another.

A school activity used colored blocks to move a character. Jordan made the character repeat a short path, then spent a whole session fixing an unwanted extra turn. They did not want to draw a background, although classmates were much more interested in adding costumes and music.

They made a tiny list for tracking borrowed books on an old tablet, then lost the file during a reset. Jordan was upset less about the appearance than about the unanswered question of why the saving step failed. Their cousin helped recover one earlier copy, but several entries remained missing.

A clinician described Jordan’s prolonged low mood, sleep disruption, and withdrawal as depression. Their mother arranged appointments when shifts allowed; their father called it too much screen time. Some weeks Jordan still enjoyed debugging small programs, and some weeks even opening the laptop felt like an unreasonable task.

In computing class they made a reminder script that sent duplicate alerts until they found a loop running twice. They liked isolating the error and disliked presenting the result with a sales-style introduction. An unfinished attendance utility stayed unfinished after a difficult month; praise did not automatically restore their momentum.

Jordan currently maintains a small household list that synchronizes when the connection returns. They enjoy making ordinary digital pieces cooperate, but resist relatives who demand a grand ambition from that fact. Appointments and support remain uneven, and they are unsure which household promises they can consistently keep.

enjoys: Tracing why a small program behaves unexpectedly
Making lists and reminders work reliably
Watching quiet comedy with their cousin
avoids: Being given responsibility without an agreed limit
activities: Helps a neighbor with simple device settings for occasional pay
demonstratedSkills: Reproduces errors with small examples
Checks saved data after changes
Writes concise notes about fixes
motivations: Removing a specific recurring annoyance
Understanding what failed
Being trusted without being overloaded
ambitions: Keep one small system working for a full term
Have enough steadiness to choose their own next commitment
practicalConstraints: Uncertain time and energy for added duties

biography.selfDescription: “The button should do the thing it says. Getting that right is satisfying. Please do not make me sell the button.”
openQuestions: What responsibility can they sustain across uneven weeks?
Would they enjoy collaborative technical work with clear boundaries?
Which current supports will remain available next term?

biography.name: Tessa Nguyen

background.family: Lives with her aunt, uncle, and two cousins; her mother works in another Texas city and calls most evenings.
background.finances: Family expenses are shared carefully; Tessa earns some spending money helping at a weekend food stall.
background.geography: A neighborhood near Galveston Bay, where drainage and weather change familiar walking routes.
background.cultureLanguages: English at school, Vietnamese at family meals; reads Vietnamese slowly.
background.school: Public school with a science club that meets inconsistently when transport and room access permit.
background.accessOpportunities: Has repeated experience recording local observations, a phone camera, borrowed reference books, and little access to specialized equipment.

timeline.story: Tessa noticed tiny shells caught in the cracks beside her aunt’s doorway and put them in a margarine tub. She forgot where several came from. Her uncle encouraged her to label the next batch, but she mostly wanted to look again after rain changed what appeared.

She watched ants avoid a wet strip on the pavement, then return by a different route. Her cousin said the ants were scared of water. Tessa repeated the observation the next afternoon and was bothered when nothing happened, although she did not yet know what to write down.

A teacher loaned her a magnifier. Tessa kept a notebook of leaves from three streets, drawing marks and recording where each leaf lay. She mixed up two specimens and crossed out a whole page. The teacher accepted the correction; Tessa still remembers it as a careless mistake.

She began recording puddle depth near the bus stop with a marked stick. After several weeks she noticed that her measuring position had shifted. She restarted, kept the old pages, and explained the difference when asked. She privately assumed a more capable person would have noticed sooner.

During a school investigation, Tessa recorded dates, repeated observations, and a possible alternative explanation that others omitted. Her group used her notes but chose another student to speak. She was relieved and disappointed together, then convinced herself that relief proved she did not understand the work well enough.

She compared shade and soil dampness in containers behind the apartment, using the same rough method over several months. A holiday interruption left a gap, which she marked instead of guessing. Her aunt praised the careful record; Tessa worried that household containers made the whole exercise too ordinary to count.

Tessa now has several years of imperfect observations and can explain why two sets should not be combined. She asks a teacher to check conclusions before saying them aloud, sometimes twice. She wants to investigate a new question independently but has not chosen one she considers worth other people’s time.

enjoys: Returning to the same place and noticing changes
Comparing explanations against dated notes
Organizing photographs after a walk
avoids: Speaking first in an unfamiliar group
activities: Records local shade and moisture changes
Helps at a weekend food stall
demonstratedSkills: Keeps dates and method changes visible
Recognizes confounding conditions
Preserves missing observations without inventing replacements
Explains limits of a comparison
unfamiliarActivities: A long investigation led entirely by her
Work away from familiar local sites
motivations: Finding out what an observation can actually support
Making a record someone else could check
ambitions: Complete one question without asking approval at every step
Have her notes taken seriously
struggles: Treating ordinary materials as evidence of low ability
practicalConstraints: Weather and family travel create observation gaps

biography.selfDescription: “I can tell you what changed in my method. I still feel like I ought to ask someone before I say what it means.”
openQuestions: What would allow her to trust a limited conclusion?
Would unfamiliar equipment increase interest or mainly worry?
How much independent responsibility does she want once speaking is optional?

biography.name: Marisol Peña

background.family: Lives with her parents, younger brother, and a cousin; neither parent attended college, and both ask practical questions about further education.
background.finances: Rent and routine bills are covered through combined wages, with little room for unpaid travel or expensive programs.
background.geography: Rio Grande Valley town near irrigated fields and growing retail strips.
background.cultureLanguages: Spanish at home and English at school; translates some ordinary written notices for relatives.
background.school: Public school with a busy biology teacher and limited laboratory supplies.
background.accessOpportunities: Public library, school reading access, backyard plants, and basic classroom experiments; no direct experience in care settings.

timeline.story: Marisol watched a scraped knee change color over several days and asked why the new surface looked different. She also pulled apart seed pods in the yard. Her mother remembers the mess more clearly than the questions, because Marisol often left the pieces on the kitchen table.

When bean plants grew at different speeds, she moved the slowest one closer to the window and forgot that she had changed its conditions. A teacher asked what else might explain the difference. Marisol began leaving little notes beside pots, though watering still happened whenever someone remembered.

She became curious about why breathing sped up after running, comparing her own recovery after different playground games. She did not make a formal record and sometimes confused effort with speed. An illustrated library book gave her new words and also made clear how many pieces she had missed.

Marisol read about digestion beyond the pages assigned in class and asked why explanations used both chemical and mechanical processes. Her teacher could answer part of the question. She copied unfamiliar words into a notebook, leaving blanks where the definitions assumed other knowledge she did not yet have.

A classroom experiment involving yeast caught her attention because a small change produced a visible difference. She repeated a rough version at home with uneven measuring spoons. She was more interested in what living systems were doing than in arranging a display, and admitted that her home comparison was unreliable.

She began borrowing books about regulation within bodies and reading beyond class even when the material was slow. Her parents worried about how long further study might take. Marisol said explicitly that many years of study would be acceptable if the subject kept opening up, although she could not explain the costs.

She now reads in short stretches between helping with dinner and a weekend paid shift packing produce. She wants deeper study of bodily and living systems and remains open to a lengthy education. She has never spent time in a care setting and cannot say whether those daily environments would suit her.

enjoys: Reading about feedback and regulation in living systems
Finding links between separate body processes
Growing plants with notes about changed conditions
Family card games
avoids: Claiming her home experiments prove too much
Being rushed to name a final destination
Graphic videos shared mainly to shock people
activities: Packs produce during some weekend shifts
demonstratedSkills: Stays with difficult reading and marks missing prerequisites
Distinguishes a rough comparison from a controlled experiment
Explains linked processes using simple drawings
motivations: Understanding how living parts maintain a changing whole
Learning enough to replace memorized fragments with explanations
ambitions: Be the first in her immediate family to complete further education
Continue studying for many years if the questions remain compelling
Take a course with more substantial laboratory access
supports: Parents encourage education while asking about costs

biography.selfDescription: “A long time studying does not scare me as much as pretending I understand something because I remembered its name.”
openQuestions: How will interest change with more rigorous practical work?
Would she enjoy the routines and interpersonal demands of care settings?
What financial and family arrangements could support lengthy study?

biography.name: Daniela Brooks

background.family: Lives with her father and stepmother during the school week and spends alternate weekends with her mother and half-sister.
background.finances: Comfortable but divided households have different spending rules and expectations about her time.
background.geography: Central Austin, with school friends scattered across neighborhoods requiring different bus connections.
background.cultureLanguages: English at home; extended family conversations include African American church traditions and differing views about public disagreement.
background.school: Public magnet program with extensive reading and frequent discussion, but limited quiet space between classes.
background.accessOpportunities: Strong library access and reliable internet; has written for a small student publication but has little experience in formal public proceedings.

timeline.story: Daniela noticed that the same board-game move was allowed at one house and forbidden at the other. She asked adults to write the rules on the box lid. Nobody did, so she drew symbols of her own and became upset when a cousin could not interpret them.

A classroom disagreement about whose turn came next ended with everyone remembering a different promise. Daniela wrote the order on scrap paper after that. She did not enjoy being the person who announced it, especially when an older child accused her of taking sides by keeping a record.

She liked stories that let two characters describe the same event differently. Her book reports grew longer because she wanted to explain why both accounts made sense from somewhere. A teacher asked for a clearer conclusion, and Daniela struggled to shorten the explanation without making one character seem foolish.

At home she drafted a proposal for sharing a game console across visiting schedules. It included exceptions for unfinished games and homework delays. Her half-sister found an exception that favored Daniela. Daniela rewrote it, but remained embarrassed that a supposedly fair rule had hidden her own convenience.

A school discussion became heated when students used the same word to mean different things. Daniela stayed silent, then wrote a careful explanation afterward. Several classmates appreciated it, while one said she should have spoken sooner. She could see the point and still dreaded the thought of interrupting the argument.

She helped edit a student publication piece about an unpopular club rule, asking the writer to distinguish what happened from what participants inferred. She removed a sharp sentence she personally agreed with because its evidence was weak. She declined an invitation to defend the piece in an assembly discussion.

Daniela currently writes patient notes about competing interpretations and checks whether a proposed rule treats similar cases similarly. She likes the revision process more than winning a live exchange. She wants her writing to matter, but is unsure how much public conflict she could accept as part of that responsibility.

enjoys: Comparing conflicting accounts
Writing explanations that preserve relevant differences
Testing fair rules against awkward examples
Reading on the bus
demonstratedSkills: Separates observation from interpretation
Finds exceptions that expose unequal rules
Revises explanations for clarity
Represents an opposing account without caricature
motivations: Making disagreement more understandable
Preventing a convenient rule from being mistaken for a fair one
ambitions: Write something useful enough that people return to it
Learn how to reach a conclusion without flattening a complicated account
struggles: Avoids speaking even when clarification might help
practicalConstraints: Unclear willingness to enforce decisions she helps explain

biography.selfDescription: “I usually have something to say after the room gets quiet. I wish that counted at the moment people decide things.”
openQuestions: Can she tolerate disagreement when a written explanation becomes consequential?
Does she want to enforce rules or mainly clarify them?
What would help her choose a defensible conclusion without endlessly revising?

biography.name: Nadia Shah

background.family: Lives with both parents and an older sister who visits from another city.
background.finances: Comfortable income, reliable transportation, and room for modest supplies.
background.cultureLanguages: Gujarati and English at home; she understands more Gujarati than she speaks.
background.school: Suburban public high school with reading accommodations for diagnosed dyslexia.
background.accessOpportunities: Tutoring, school clubs, library sewing machines, and family help obtaining materials.

timeline.story: Nadia liked fitting shapes into a wooden puzzle and putting scarves on stuffed animals. Adults praised how quickly she recognized matching shapes. She avoided books with crowded pages but listened happily to stories, especially when she could interrupt to ask why a character wore a certain outfit.

Reading lessons were frustrating and sometimes ended with her pretending to need the bathroom. Her dyslexia was identified, and individual instruction helped slowly. She liked number patterns at school, but at home she spent longer fastening scraps around dolls with tape than completing extra puzzle sheets.

Her father bought a large mathematics workbook after she enjoyed a classroom challenge. Nadia liked some pages and quietly skipped others. At a cousin’s house she learned to thread a blunt needle, made crooked stitches, and returned the next weekend specifically to finish a tiny drawstring bag.

She followed short sewing videos repeatedly because written directions were tiring. She cut one piece backward and hid it for a week before asking for help. Her mathematics work remained strong with spoken explanations available, and relatives began describing that subject as the obvious thing she should keep pursuing.

Nadia joined a mathematics club after her parents suggested it. She usually solved her share and liked one teammate, but rarely thought about problems afterward. She used free evenings to alter an oversized shirt, unpicking the same seam repeatedly because the fabric pulled in a way she disliked.

A classmate asked her to mend a torn pocket. Nadia enjoyed figuring out the lining but found the expectation of a perfect result stressful. Her parents offered an additional mathematics course, and she accepted without much enthusiasm. She spent the first weekend drawing sleeve variations in the margins of its schedule.

Nadia still earns strong mathematics marks and does not resent the subject itself. Given a free afternoon, she usually chooses fabric experiments or clothing sketches. She has told her mother this once, then softened the statement when questioned. She has little experience sewing under deadlines and no desire to promise expertise.

enjoys: Changing the shape of an ordinary garment
Testing how fabric hangs
Some geometry problems
Audiobooks during repetitive stitching
demonstratedSkills: Strong algebra and spatial reasoning
Patiently unpicks and revises seams
Uses video and spoken directions effectively
unfamiliarActivities: Choosing most of her own course schedule
motivations: Wants time for activities she chooses herself
Likes a visible change she can wear
ambitions: Finish a jacket lining without her sister taking over
Explain her preferences more clearly at home
struggles: Agrees before considering her own interest
supports: Parents who provide resources even when they misunderstand her preferences
practicalConstraints: Shared family plans limit some weekends
Needs accessible formats for lengthy instructions

biography.selfDescription: Math comes easier than reading, and I like being good at it. That is different from what I go do when nobody tells me. I am also not as careful with sewing as people assume; there are unfinished things everywhere.
openQuestions: How consistently will she express her own preference?
Would she enjoy making things for others on a schedule?
Which mathematics activities are personally interesting?
variationTags: family expectation differs from voluntary activity

biography.name: Miles Bennett

background.family: Lives with both parents and a younger sister; nearby grandparents visit often.
background.geography: A quiet neighborhood in Round Rock, Texas.
background.cultureLanguages: English-speaking household with familiar family holiday traditions and no strong religious involvement.
background.school: Public high school with accessible teachers and several laboratory classes.
background.accessOpportunities: Reliable computer, rides, occasional tutoring, clubs, and ordinary family vacations.

timeline.story: Miles liked building short ramps for toy cars but usually asked an adult to fix them when the cars fell off. He also watched cartoons and played restaurant with his sister. His parents remember an easygoing child who sometimes abandoned a game as soon as somebody changed the rules.

He enjoyed a classroom experiment using magnets and asked for a kit afterward. Most pieces ended up mixed with other toys. He liked having his grandfather demonstrate things one step at a time, but did not spontaneously write observations or develop projects beyond the instructions provided.

Miles spent more time swimming and trading game cards than doing science activities. A broken flashlight interested him for one afternoon, although his mother completed the repair. He was embarrassed when classmates finished multiplication faster and needed reassurance before agreeing to practice where anyone could hear him.

At home during remote school, he watched videos about motion and paused them to copy diagrams. The mathematics often escaped him. He asked his father questions, got irritated when the answer seemed too quick, and returned later. He also ignored several assignments whose instructions he understood perfectly well.

An introductory physics unit interested him enough to attempt optional problems. His first answers were mostly wrong. A teacher showed him how to draw the situation before choosing an equation, and he began using that routine. He liked the small improvement but still needed help recognizing which quantities mattered.

Miles chose a demanding physical science class with his parents’ support. He attended extra help repeatedly and sometimes took twice as long as friends on homework. He enjoyed tracing where his reasoning failed. He disliked the report formatting and occasionally let a classmate do too much of the shared writing.

He voluntarily continues with physics even after an uneven examination result. He asks for hints, tries another approach, and sometimes needs someone to work the entire example beside him. He likes the effort when it makes a confusing idea clearer, but cannot yet tell whether he would enjoy prolonged independent work.

enjoys: Understanding motion problems after several attempts
Comparing an experiment with his prediction
Swimming casually
Board games with family
activities: Works through practice examples with a tutor
Plays games with friends most weekends
demonstratedSkills: Returns to difficult questions after frustration
Uses diagrams more consistently
Asks specific questions about a mistaken step
motivations: Enjoys the moment a difficult explanation makes sense
Wants to see what practice can change
ambitions: Complete the next physics course
Solve a whole unfamiliar problem without a hint eventually
struggles: Can depend too much on a partner for writing
Sometimes mistakes familiarity with an example for understanding
practicalConstraints: Homework takes time from other activities
Needs to schedule help before class deadlines

biography.selfDescription: I am the person still doing problem two when my friend finishes the page. I actually want to keep doing it most days. I do not know if that counts as being good at it, and I get annoyed when people act like trying makes it easy.
openQuestions: How will interest hold up when support is less immediate?
Does he enjoy experimental work as much as worked problems?
Which writing responsibilities will he take independently?

biography.name: Diego Moreno

background.family: Lives with his father, stepmother, and two younger siblings; his mother lives nearby.
background.finances: Stable modest income; small supplies are possible if planned.
background.cultureLanguages: Spanish and English across both homes; relatives regularly cross between different family traditions.
background.school: Neighborhood public high school with several clubs he has chosen not to join.
background.accessOpportunities: Public library, a basic phone camera, family rides when arranged, and inexpensive paper supplies.

timeline.story: Diego liked folding paper into small houses and placing a toy animal inside. He resisted joining cousins in loud chase games, sometimes sitting beside his mother instead. Adults remember him as stubborn, but he did enjoy a calm game of hiding objects when nobody made it a competition.

A classroom animation using cutout shapes caught his attention. At home he moved a paper dog across a table while his father took pictures. He disliked being filmed himself. His first sequence barely moved when played back, and he abandoned it until his father showed him how to take more photographs.

He made another paper sequence about a hat blowing away, using a borrowed tablet. His cousins offered to provide voices, but he preferred silent motion and declined. He tried a team sport for several weeks, disliked practices and games, and was relieved when his parents accepted that answer.

Remote school left him making tiny stop-motion clips beside the kitchen window. Some clips were only six seconds long. He liked changing the spacing between frames and did not like writing stories about the characters. He also avoided online multiplayer games because the constant conversation and competition annoyed him.

A teacher suggested drama, drawing club, and a group video activity after seeing one clip. Diego tried drawing club twice and disliked the shared prompts. He declined drama outright. He kept making short paper movements at home, even though adults worried that his narrow choices meant he was missing something.

He spent a month making a folded bird turn its head convincingly. Several versions looked worse than the first, and he left the materials untouched for days. A friend wanted a longer funny film together. Diego refused because planning dialogue and negotiating scenes sounded unpleasant, though the refusal strained their friendship.

Diego makes brief silent paper animations when he wants to, sometimes once a week and sometimes less. He dislikes sports, public performing, persuasion, group planning, and most assigned creative prompts from actual experience. He does not want to choose an alternative merely to seem agreeable, but admits he has barely tried many solitary activities.

enjoys: Changing frame spacing in very short paper animations
Quiet music while cutting shapes
Walking familiar routes alone in daylight
activities: Watches a few animation process videos
demonstratedSkills: Notices small differences in movement between frames
Repeats a short sequence to improve timing
States a preference clearly even when others disagree
unfamiliarActivities: Making a project for someone else’s specifications
motivations: Likes controlling a tiny movement until it looks right
Wants adults to accept a sincere refusal
ambitions: Make a paper bird land without its wing wobbling
Keep a folder of clips he likes
struggles: Avoids discussing why he dislikes something
Stops working when revisions become irritating
supports: Father who lends a phone stand
Mother who keeps a supply envelope for him
One friend who watches clips without requesting a bigger project
practicalConstraints: Phone needed by family at times
Limited storage for fragile paper pieces

biography.selfDescription: I have tried some of the things people keep suggesting, and I did not like them. Making a paper thing move is different. I am not saying I know every possible thing I like, but I am not going to say I want a club just to end the conversation.
openQuestions: Which unfamiliar solitary activities would he willingly try?
How much of the animation process remains appealing under external requirements?
Can he express refusals while maintaining friendships?

biography.name: Imani Carter

background.family: Lives with her grandmother and father; her older cousin is a frequent visitor.
background.finances: Generally stable essentials, with little room for expensive equipment.
background.geography: Beaumont, Texas, with a recent move to a different neighborhood.
background.cultureLanguages: English-speaking Black family with strong church and neighborhood ties; her own participation varies.
background.school: Public high school; recently changed electives after a semester of uncertainty.
background.accessOpportunities: Library computers, a borrowed audio recorder, family cooking supplies, and school-day clubs.

timeline.story: Imani liked helping her grandmother stir cake batter and would tell visitors she had made the entire cake. She also drew street signs on cardboard for toy cars. Her family mostly remembers the kitchen stories because they took photographs there, and Imani is unsure which activity she actually chose more.

She enjoyed measuring ingredients and decorating cupcakes, especially when cousins came over. Cleanup reliably caused an argument. On walks she asked why particular streets ended suddenly, but forgot the answers. Her teacher called her enthusiastic, a description that fit her first attempt at nearly anything better than the fourth.

A school baking display made Imani proud, although her grandmother had rescued a failed batch the night before. For several months she requested recipe books. She also copied neighborhood routes into a notebook, which nobody treated as a hobby and which she later used for spelling practice.

During remote lessons she baked often and recorded short recipe introductions on a phone. Watching them now, she notices she enjoyed speaking more than repeating recipes carefully. Her father remembers her interest in ingredients, while her grandmother remembers needing to remind her about almost every cooling and cleaning step.

Imani said she wanted to spend all her free time baking, then gradually stopped doing it unless someone joined her. She blamed the small kitchen and may have been right in part. She began photographing mismatched sidewalks after rain and labeling where puddles blocked a direct walk to the bus stop.

After moving neighborhoods, she tried recording relatives’ accounts of places that had changed. She liked asking follow-up questions but left recordings unlabeled. She dropped a food-related elective and told one friend she was bored, while telling her grandmother the timetable was the problem. Both explanations contained some truth.

Imani now says mapping neighborhood changes feels more interesting than baking. She has two rough maps, three incomplete recordings, and weeks without progress. She still enjoys making one familiar cake with her grandmother. She cannot yet tell whether the change reflects lasting curiosity, wanting independence, novelty, or some combination she has not understood.

enjoys: Comparing old and current neighborhood routes
Asking relatives what used to occupy a familiar place
Making one familiar cake with her grandmother
Choosing titles for unfinished projects
avoids: Being asked to defend every changed preference
activities: Occasionally records family recollections with permission
Walks to a new bus stop
demonstratedSkills: Asks follow-up questions in a familiar conversation
Notices route details such as puddles and missing sidewalk sections
Measures familiar recipes accurately with reminders
unfamiliarActivities: Finishing and checking a complete map
Maintaining the same independent project over a year
motivations: Wants something that feels like her own choice
Curious about the changed neighborhood
Likes sharing an interesting discovery
ambitions: Finish one readable neighborhood map
Label existing recordings before making more
struggles: Accounts of her interests vary with the listener
Poor follow-through on labeling and checking
Unsure which part of past baking she enjoyed
supports: Teacher who allowed an elective change
practicalConstraints: Walking routes limited by transport and weather
Borrowed recorder must be returned regularly

biography.selfDescription: I keep saying I used to be into baking and now I am into maps, but that sounds more organized than it is. I still like the cake part with Grandma. Maybe I like collecting ideas better than finishing them. I want longer to see.
openQuestions: Will mapping interest persist after the move feels familiar?
Which unfinished work will she voluntarily return to?
What did she enjoy about baking when nobody was watching?
How much do family expectations shape her descriptions?
